name: Einstein-Infeld-Hoffmann Field of Many Bodies
description: The gravitational field of $N$ slowly moving bodies to the first order beyond Newton, the order at which the vacuum field equations fix how the bodies move. It is an approximate spacetime with a definite metric, the one the planets and the binary pulsar are timed in.
convention: We keep factors of $c$ explicit and count $v/c$ as first order, so $U$ and $\chi$ are of second order, $V_1$, $V_2$, and $V_3$ of third, and $\psi$ of fourth, and we write the metric and its inverse whole. A component of the connection, the Riemann tensor, or the Ricci tensor is kept through the fourth order with two time indices or more, the third with one, and the second with none, the Einstein tensor, the Weyl tensor, and the Ricci scalar through the second, or the third with an odd number of time indices, and the Kretschmann scalar through the fourth. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: The calculation was too long to print [einstein1938]. Albert Einstein, Leopold Infeld, and Banesh Hoffmann, whose paper left the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton in June 1937 with the results alone, deposited "the entire computation" with the secretary of the School of Mathematics, "so as to be available for reference" [einstein1938]. They had asked "the fundamentally simple question of the extent to which the relativistic equations of gravitation determine the motion of ponderable bodies" [einstein1938]. Other field theories take two laws, one for how a body sources the field and a separate force law for how a body moves in it [kennefick1999]. Einstein had conjectured since 1927, when he wrote on it with Jakob Grommer, that in general relativity the field equations alone fix how the bodies move [kennefick1999].¶Their bodies are points where the field of empty space becomes singular, so no assumption about what matter is made of comes in [einstein1938]. The bodies move slowly: a speed over the speed of light counts as one small step and a gravitational potential as two, and the vacuum equations are solved one step at a time in the space between the points [einstein1938]. At each step a solution exists only if the points move in a particular way [einstein1938]. The first step returns Newton's law of gravitation, "from the field equations alone, without extra assumption such as was hitherto believed to be necessary and was supplied by the law of geodetic lines" [einstein1938]. The second ran to "forty-one different types of term" and gave the first relativistic correction to the motion of two massive bodies, "the main result of our calculations from the point of view of practical application" [einstein1938].¶The same calculation fixes the field between the bodies, to the same accuracy as their motion [einstein1938]. With each mass written as a length, $m_a = GM_a/c^2$, at the distance $r_a$ and moving at the velocity $\mathbf{v}_a$, it is $ds^2 = -\left(1 - 2U + 2U^2 - 2\psi - \sum_a m_a\,\partial_t^2 r_a/c^2\right)c^2dt^2 - 8\,\mathbf{V}\cdot d\mathbf{x}\,c\,dt + \left(1 + 2U\right)d\mathbf{x}^2$ in their coordinates, which are harmonic to this order, where $U = \sum_a m_a/r_a$ is Newton's potential over $c^2$, $\mathbf{V} = \sum_a m_a\mathbf{v}_a/(c\,r_a)$, and $\psi = \sum_a (m_a/r_a)\left(3v_a^2/2c^2 - \sum_{b \neq a} m_b/r_{ab}\right)$ with $r_{ab}$ the distance between two bodies [einstein1938, blanchet1998]. In $\psi$ each mass is raised by its own motion and lowered by the pull of its neighbours, which they called "the first relativistic corrections to the masses" [einstein1938]. The term in $\mathbf{V}$ is the gravitomagnetic field of the moving bodies, which pulls on whatever moves past them [will2018]. No wave leaves at this order: their method, they wrote, "cannot lead to the conclusion that in the circular motion of two point masses energy is radiated to infinity in the form of waves" [einstein1938].¶The first steps of the calculation were twenty years old [einstein1938, will2014]. Hendrik Lorentz and Johannes Droste, and separately Willem de Sitter, had derived the metric and the equations of motion of $N$ bodies to this order in 1916 and 1917, and de Sitter's equations carried errors [will2014]. From de Sitter's equations Tullio Levi-Civita concluded in 1937 that a double star of unequal masses on an eccentric orbit accelerates itself, its centre of mass speeding up toward the pericentre of the orbit, and he suggested looking for the effect in nearby close binaries [will2014, levicivita1937]. Arthur Eddington and G. L. Clark showed that the effect vanishes once de Sitter's equations are corrected [will2014, eddington1938]. Howard Robertson integrated the equations of Einstein, Infeld, and Hoffmann for two bodies of comparable mass: the centre of mass stays put, and the long axis of the orbit turns, as Mercury's does, at a rate set by the sum of the two masses [einstein1938, robertson1938, will2014, kopeikin2020].¶Is a star a point? In the calculation of 1938 the inner structure of a body dropped out, as long as the field near it was close to spherical [will2014]. Two black holes that move slowly and far apart follow equations of motion of the same kind, which Peter D'Eath derived in 1975 using only the vacuum equations [death1975]. A test had arrived the year before, when Russell Hulse and Joseph Taylor found the pulsar PSR B1913+16 circling an unseen companion every $7.75$ hours [hulse1975, will2014]. Its orbit turns in its own plane by $4.226598$ degrees a year, about $35{,}000$ times the rate of Mercury's $42.98$ seconds of arc a century [will2014]. That rate measures the total mass, and with one more relativistic effect in the timing of the pulses it weighs the two stars at $1.4398$ and $1.3886$ solar masses [will2014].¶The equations of motion for $N$ bodies, with Eddington's numbers $\beta$ and $\gamma$ put in front of their terms, are the basis of the codes that compute the orbits of the planets and of spacecraft [will2018]. One effect in them went uncalculated until 2018, when Clifford Will showed that cross terms between the Sun's pull on Mercury and the pulls of the other planets, together with the gravitomagnetic field of the moving planets, turn Mercury's perihelion by a few parts in a million of its $42.98$ seconds of arc a century, within reach of the BepiColombo orbiters [will2018]. Luc Blanchet, Guillaume Faye, and Bénédicte Ponsot carried the field of two bodies to higher order and proposed it as initial data for simulating two black holes on a computer [blanchet1998]. Kashif Alvi joined it to a tidally distorted black hole around each point [alvi2000]. In Alvi's construction the field of Einstein, Infeld, and Hoffmann fills the region from the distance $\sqrt{m_a d}$ of each hole, for two holes a distance $d$ apart, out to $c/2\Omega$, with $\Omega$ the angular velocity of the orbit, where the radiation zone begins [alvi2000].

related.text: One body at rest, with Eddington's numbers in front of its terms. With $U = m/r$ and nothing moving, the standard gauge here is that metric at $\beta = \gamma = 1$ [will2014].

One body at rest. With $U = m/r$ and every other potential zero the metric is Schwarzschild's in isotropic coordinates, expanded far from the horizon, and Einstein, Infeld, and Hoffmann took the field close to each body to be of that kind [will2014].
The other field of many bodies. There each body carries a charge equal to its mass, and all of them stay at rest for good; here nothing holds the bodies apart, so they orbit.

parameters.description: Newton's potential of the bodies over $c^2$, a pure number: $U = \sum_a m_a/r_a$ for bodies of mass $M_a$ at the places $\mathbf{x}_a$, with $m_a = GM_a/c^2$ the mass of body $a$ as a length and $r_a = |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_a|$ the distance to it; between the bodies it solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_x^2U + \partial_y^2U + \partial_z^2U = 0$

Post-Newtonian potential, a pure number: $\psi = \sum_a \left(m_a/r_a\right)\left(3v_a^2/2c^2 - \sum_{b \neq a} m_b/r_{ab}\right)$, with $v_a$ the speed of body $a$ and $r_{ab} = |\mathbf{x}_a - \mathbf{x}_b|$ the distance between two bodies; between the bodies it solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_x^2\psi + \partial_y^2\psi + \partial_z^2\psi = 0$
Superpotential, an area: $\chi = \sum_a m_a r_a$, which solves $\partial_x^2\chi + \partial_y^2\chi + \partial_z^2\chi = 2U$

Component along $x$ of the vector potential $\mathbf{V} = \sum_a m_a\mathbf{v}_a/(c\,r_a)$, a pure number, with $\mathbf{v}_a$ the velocity of body $a$; between the bodies it solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_x^2V_1 + \partial_y^2V_1 + \partial_z^2V_1 = 0$
Component along $y$ of $\mathbf{V}$, a pure number; between the bodies it solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_x^2V_2 + \partial_y^2V_2 + \partial_z^2V_2 = 0$

Component along $z$ of $\mathbf{V}$, a pure number; between the bodies it solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_x^2V_3 + \partial_y^2V_3 + \partial_z^2V_3 = 0$, and the three components keep $\partial_tU + \partial_xV_1 + \partial_yV_2 + \partial_zV_3 = 0$, since each mass is constant

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$ of Einstein, Infeld, and Hoffmann, which are harmonic to this order, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, so $\partial_t$ and a dot on $t$ in the geodesic equations mean derivatives along $ct$. A derivative along $t$ counts one order more than what it acts on, since the bodies move slowly.

parameters.description: Newton's potential of the bodies over $c^2$, a pure number: $U = \sum_a m_a/r_a$ for bodies of mass $M_a$ at the places $\mathbf{x}_a$, with $m_a = GM_a/c^2$ the mass of body $a$ as a length and $r_a = |\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_a|$ the distance to it; between the bodies it solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_x^2U + \partial_y^2U + \partial_z^2U = 0$

Post-Newtonian potential, a pure number: $\psi = \sum_a \left(m_a/r_a\right)\left(3v_a^2/2c^2 - \sum_{b \neq a} m_b/r_{ab}\right)$, with $v_a$ the speed of body $a$ and $r_{ab} = |\mathbf{x}_a - \mathbf{x}_b|$ the distance between two bodies; between the bodies it solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_x^2\psi + \partial_y^2\psi + \partial_z^2\psi = 0$
Superpotential, an area: $\chi = \sum_a m_a r_a$, which solves $\partial_x^2\chi + \partial_y^2\chi + \partial_z^2\chi = 2U$

Component along $x$ of the vector potential $\mathbf{V} = \sum_a m_a\mathbf{v}_a/(c\,r_a)$, a pure number, with $\mathbf{v}_a$ the velocity of body $a$; between the bodies it solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_x^2V_1 + \partial_y^2V_1 + \partial_z^2V_1 = 0$
Component along $y$ of $\mathbf{V}$, a pure number; between the bodies it solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_x^2V_2 + \partial_y^2V_2 + \partial_z^2V_2 = 0$

Component along $z$ of $\mathbf{V}$, a pure number; between the bodies it solves Laplace's equation, $\partial_x^2V_3 + \partial_y^2V_3 + \partial_z^2V_3 = 0$, and the three components keep $\partial_tU + \partial_xV_1 + \partial_yV_2 + \partial_zV_3 = 0$, since each mass is constant

coordinates.convention: We use the coordinates $(t, x, y, z)$ of the standard post-Newtonian gauge, whose time is the harmonic time less $\partial_t\chi/2c$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, so $\partial_t$ and a dot on $t$ in the geodesic equations mean derivatives along $ct$. A derivative along $t$ counts one order more than what it acts on, since the bodies move slowly.
